title: Energy, Work & Power
description: Energy stores and transfers, conservation of energy, work done, power, efficiency, Sankey diagrams, and energy resources.

notes.heading: Energy Stores and Transfers
notes.body: Energy exists in different stores: Kinetic (motion, KE=½mv²), Gravitational potential (height, GPE=mgh), Elastic potential (stretched/compressed), Chemical (fuels, food, batteries), Thermal (internal energy of particles), Nuclear (atomic nucleus), Magnetic, Electrostatic. Energy is transferred between stores by four pathways: Mechanical work (forces moving objects), Electrical work (current transferring energy), Heating (temperature difference), Radiation (light, sound waves). Energy is measured in joules (J). 1 kJ = 1000 J. A system is an object or group of objects. In a closed system, no energy enters or leaves — total energy is constant. Open systems exchange energy with surroundings.

illustration.alt: Energy stores diagram and a Sankey diagram showing energy transfer in a light bulb.
illustration.caption: Energy is transferred between stores; it is never created or destroyed.

notes.heading: Conservation of Energy and Sankey Diagrams
notes.body: The Law of Conservation of Energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores or dissipated (spread out) to the surroundings. Total energy in a closed system remains constant. Sankey diagrams show energy transfers visually: arrow width represents energy amount. The input arrow splits into useful output(s) and wasted output(s). Wasted energy is usually transferred as thermal energy to the surroundings (dissipated). Examples: Light bulb — electrical → light (useful) + heat (wasted). Car engine — chemical (fuel) → kinetic (useful, ~25%) + heat + sound (wasted, ~75%). Dissipated energy is NOT destroyed — it spreads into the surroundings, becoming less useful (lower temperature, more spread out).

illustration.alt: Energy stores diagram and a Sankey diagram showing energy transfer in a light bulb.
illustration.caption: A Sankey diagram shows useful energy output vs wasted energy — width of arrows is proportional to energy.

notes.heading: Work Done and Power
notes.body: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance. Work done (J) = Force (N) × Distance moved in direction of force (m). W = Fd. If the force and movement are in different directions, only the component of force in the direction of movement does work. 1 joule = work done when 1 N force moves through 1 m. Power is the rate of energy transfer (or rate of doing work). P = E/t = W/t (watts, W). 1 W = 1 J/s. A 100 W bulb transfers 100 J of energy every second. P = Fv for constant velocity (power = force × velocity). Example: car engine produces 20,000 W at 25 m/s → driving force = P/v = 800 N.

illustration.alt: Diagram of a person pushing a box, illustrating work done = force × distance, and the power formula.
illustration.caption: Work done equals the energy transferred when a force moves an object.

notes.heading: Efficiency
notes.body: Efficiency = (useful output energy ÷ total input energy) × 100%. Nothing is 100% efficient — some energy is always transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings. Efficiency can be expressed as a ratio (0-1) or percentage (0-100%). Ways to improve efficiency: lubrication (reduce friction), thermal insulation (reduce heat loss), streamlining (reduce air resistance), using more efficient designs (LED vs incandescent bulbs). Sankey diagrams visually show efficiency — the useful energy arrow as a proportion of total input. Example: motor takes 500 J electrical, outputs 400 J kinetic. Efficiency = 400/500 = 0.8 = 80%. 100 J is wasted as heat/sound.

illustration.alt: Energy input, useful output, and wasted energy for an electric motor, with efficiency calculation.
illustration.caption: Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to total input. No device is 100 percent efficient.

notes.heading: Energy Resources: Renewable vs Non-Renewable
notes.body: Non-renewable resources are finite — they will run out. (1) Fossil fuels — coal, oil, natural gas. Formed from ancient organisms over millions of years. Burned to release chemical energy → thermal → kinetic (turbines) → electrical. Advantages: reliable, high energy density, existing infrastructure. Disadvantages: CO₂ emissions (climate change), SO₂ (acid rain), finite, environmental damage from extraction. (2) Nuclear — uranium/plutonium fission releases enormous energy. Advantages: no CO₂, very high energy density, reliable baseload. Disadvantages: radioactive waste (storage for thousands of years), risk of catastrophic accidents, expensive decommissioning. Renewable resources are replenished on a human timescale: Solar (photovoltaic cells, solar heating), Wind (turbines), Hydroelectric (dams), Tidal/Wave, Geothermal, Biomass. Advantages: no CO₂ during operation, renewable, energy security. Disadvantages: intermittent (solar — night/clouds; wind — calm days), visual/noise impact, habitat disruption, high initial costs.

illustration.alt: Comparison of renewable and non-renewable energy resources, including fossil fuels, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro, and tidal.
illustration.caption: Renewable resources will not run out but may be weather-dependent; non-renewable resources are finite.

notes.heading: Thermal Energy Transfer: Conduction, Convection, Radiation
notes.body: Thermal energy transfers from hot to cold regions by three mechanisms: (1) Conduction — transfer through a solid by vibrating particles passing energy along. Metals conduct well (free electrons aid transfer). Non-metals/poor conductors (insulators — wood, plastic, air). (2) Convection — transfer in fluids (liquids/gases). Heated fluid expands → less dense → rises. Cooler, denser fluid sinks → convection current. Examples: sea breezes, radiator heating rooms, mantle convection (plate tectonics). (3) Radiation — transfer by infrared electromagnetic waves. Does NOT need particles — can travel through a vacuum (Sun's energy reaches Earth). All hot objects emit infrared. Dark, matt surfaces absorb and emit radiation well. Light, shiny surfaces reflect radiation (poor absorbers/emitters). Applications: vacuum flasks (minimise all three), clothing choices (white in summer reflects; black in winter absorbs), building insulation (loft insulation traps air — poor conductor).

illustration.alt: Three methods of thermal energy transfer: conduction in solids, convection in fluids, and radiation through electromagnetic waves.
illustration.caption: Conduction requires a medium; convection occurs in fluids; radiation can travel through a vacuum.

notes.heading: Specific Heat Capacity
notes.body: Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy required to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. ΔE = mcΔθ. Units: J/(kg·°C). Water: c = 4200 J/(kg·°C) — very high; it heats up and cools down slowly. This is why coastal climates are moderate (sea acts as thermal buffer) and water is used in central heating and car cooling systems. Practical: use a joulemeter or electrical heater (measure P and t → E = Pt) to supply known energy to a metal block. Measure temperature rise. Calculate c = E/(m×Δθ). Compare with accepted values. Sources of error: heat loss to surroundings (use insulation), thermometer lag, incomplete mixing. The high specific heat capacity of water is crucial for life — oceans absorb/release heat slowly, moderating Earth's climate.

illustration.alt: Experimental setup for measuring specific heat capacity with a metal block, heater, and thermometer, plus the formula ΔE = mcΔθ.
illustration.caption: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by one degree Celsius.

flashcards.definition: Energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Doubling speed quadruples KE.
flashcards.example: 2 kg ball at 3 m/s: KE = ½×2×9 = 9 J.

flashcards.definition: Energy due to height in gravitational field: GPE = mgh.
flashcards.example: 5 kg on 2 m shelf: GPE = 5×10×2 = 100 J.

flashcards.definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. Total energy in a closed system is constant.
(Useful output energy ÷ total input energy) × 100%. Always <100% — some energy always dissipated.
flashcards.example: 500 J in, 400 J useful out: efficiency = 80%.

flashcards.definition: W = Fd. Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance. Measured in joules (J).
flashcards.example: 10 N force moves object 3 m: W = 30 J.

flashcards.definition: Rate of energy transfer: P = E/t = W/t (watts, W). 1 W = 1 J/s.
flashcards.example: Motor transfers 500 J in 5 s: P = 100 W.

flashcards.definition: Energy to raise 1 kg by 1°C. ΔE = mcΔθ. Water: c = 4200 J/(kg·°C).
flashcards.example: Heating 2 kg water by 10°C: E = 2×4200×10 = 84,000 J.

flashcards.definition: Heat transfer through solids by particle vibration. Metals conduct well (free electrons).
flashcards.example: Metal spoon in hot soup — handle becomes hot by conduction.

flashcards.definition: Heat transfer in fluids by movement of heated (less dense) fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking.
flashcards.example: Radiator heats air → warm air rises → circulates room — convection current.

flashcards.definition: Electromagnetic wave heat transfer. No medium needed. Dark matt surfaces = best absorbers/emitters.
flashcards.example: Solar panels are black to maximise absorption of Sun's infrared radiation.

flashcards.definition: Energy from sources replenished on a human timescale: solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass.
flashcards.example: Wind turbines convert kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy.

flashcards.definition: Energy spread out to surroundings, usually as thermal energy — not destroyed, but no longer useful.
flashcards.example: Friction dissipates kinetic energy as heat — rubbing hands together warms them.

questions.stem: 3 kg ball at 4 m/s. KE?
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv² = ½×3×16 = 24 J.

questions.stem: Lamp: 100 J in, 20 J light out. Efficiency?
questions.explanation: 20/100 × 100 = 20%. 80 J is wasted as heat.

questions.stem: Falling ball: energy transformation?
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential → kinetic as height decreases and speed increases.

questions.stem: Correct energy statement:
choices: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred/dissipated
questions.explanation: Law of conservation of energy.

questions.stem: 10 kg box lifted 3 m. GPE? (g=10)
Motor lifts 200 N weight 5 m in 10 s. Power?
500 g water heated from 20°C to 50°C. Energy? (c=4200)
Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden one at same temperature?
choices: Metal conducts heat away from your hand faster (better conductor)
Metal has lower specific heat capacity
questions.explanation: Both are at room temp. Metal's high thermal conductivity rapidly transfers heat from your warm hand → feels cold.

questions.stem: Which surface is the best ABSORBER of infrared radiation?
choices: Dark and matt (absorbs most; also best emitter)
questions.explanation: Dark, matt surfaces absorb well AND emit well. Shiny, light surfaces reflect radiation.

questions.stem: Advantage of renewable over non-renewable?
choices: Will not run out — replenished naturally
questions.explanation: Renewables are replenished. Non-renewables (fossil fuels, nuclear) are finite.

questions.stem: Convection occurs in:
choices: Fluids (liquids and gases) — heated fluid rises, cooler fluid sinks
questions.explanation: Convection requires fluid movement (density changes with temperature). Solids cannot convect — particles are fixed.

questions.stem: Sankey diagram: input 800 J, useful 200 J. Width of wasted arrow?
questions.explanation: Input = useful + wasted. 800 = 200 + wasted → wasted = 600 J.

questions.stem: A 2 kg mass moving at 6 m/s. Speed doubles to 12 m/s. KE increases by:
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv². When v doubles, KE quadruples (2²=4). This is why high-speed crashes are so destructive.

questions.stem: Why is water used as a coolant in car engines?
choices: Water has a high specific heat capacity — absorbs lots of heat with small temperature rise
Water is a good electrical conductor
questions.explanation: High c means water can absorb large amounts of waste heat from the engine without its temperature rising dangerously.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a way to reduce heat loss from a house?
choices: Opening all windows — increases convection heat loss
questions.explanation: Opening windows increases heat loss by convection (warm air escapes). All other options reduce heat transfer.

questions.stem: A stretched rubber band is released and flies across the room. Main energy transfer?
questions.explanation: The stretched band stores elastic potential energy, which is transferred to kinetic energy of motion when released.

questions.stem: A swinging pendulum gradually slows and stops. What happened to its energy?
choices: It was transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy (dissipated)
It is stored permanently in the string
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed; air resistance and friction dissipate it as thermal energy to the surroundings.

questions.stem: Which of these is a NON-renewable energy resource?
choices: Natural gas — a finite fossil fuel
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel that will run out; wind, solar and hydro are replenished on a human timescale.

questions.stem: Which change reduces heat loss from a house?
choices: Fitting thicker loft insulation — traps air, a poor conductor
Replacing thick curtains with thin ones
questions.explanation: Trapped air is a poor conductor, so loft insulation slows conduction of heat through the roof. The other options all increase heat loss.

questions.stem: Why does a tiled floor feel colder than a carpeted floor in the same room?
choices: Tiles are always at a lower temperature
Tiles conduct heat away from your feet faster (better conductor)
questions.explanation: Both floors are at room temperature; tile's higher thermal conductivity draws heat from your skin faster, so it feels colder.

questions.stem: Why do coastal regions usually have milder climates than inland regions?
choices: Sea water has a high specific heat capacity — it heats up and cools down slowly
The sea reflects all incoming sunlight
Land cannot store any thermal energy
Waves generate heat at the coast
questions.explanation: Water's high c means the sea absorbs and releases large amounts of energy with only small temperature changes, moderating coastal temperatures.

questions.stem: Crane lifts a 300 N crate 4 m in 6 s. Power?
questions.explanation: W = Fd = 300×4 = 1200 J. P = W/t = 1200/6 = 200 W. (50 W forgets the distance; 1200 W forgets the time.)

questions.stem: 2 kg water heated from 25°C to 45°C. Energy? (c=4200)
A car triples its speed from 10 m/s to 30 m/s. Its kinetic energy increases by:
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv². Tripling v multiplies KE by 3² = 9 — a key reason high-speed collisions are far more destructive.
